paper_context.research_question: Can an unsupervised graph-based keyphrase extraction method that incorporates information from all occurrence positions of words (position-weighting) together with frequency improve keyphrase extraction from scholarly documents compared to PageRank-based and other strong baselines?
main_claims: PositionRank, a position-biased PageRank that weights candidate words by the inverse of each occurrence position (summed across occurrences), yields substantially better keyphrase extraction performance than PageRank variants (TextRank, SingleRank) that ignore position.
Aggregating position information from all occurrences of a word (PositionRank-full) outperforms using only the first occurrence position.

PositionRank outperforms several strong unsupervised baselines (TF-IDF, ExpandRank, TopicalPageRank) on three scholarly-paper datasets, with relative improvements in MRR up to ~29% and statistically significant gains in P/R/F1 (paired t-test, p < 0.05).
PositionRank is parameter-robust to window size and damping factor choices (performance does not change significantly across tested values).
PositionRank is simpler and computationally cheaper than topic-based or neighborhood-expanded approaches (e.g., TopicalPageRank, ExpandRank) while achieving better or comparable performance.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Effectiveness in ranking/extraction metrics: MRR, Precision, Recall, F1 at various top-k (e.g., k=1..10, top2/4/6/8).
Statistical significance of performance differences (paired t-test reported).
Ablation comparing full position-aggregation vs first-position-only to isolate the contribution of position aggregation.
Robustness to hyperparameters: window size w and PageRank damping factor α.
Comparison to a range of baselines including PageRank variants (TextRank/SingleRank), TF-IDF, ExpandRank, and TopicalPageRank.
Dataset diversity/generalizability across multiple scholarly collections (KDD, WWW, Nguyen).
Computational/complexity considerations relative to baselines (claimed lower complexity than topic models or neighborhood expansion).

extracted_claims.claim_label: PositionRank leverages position+frequency in biased PageRank
extracted_claims.claim_text: PositionRank is an unsupervised graph-based model that incorporates information from all positions of a word's occurrences (via inverse-position weights summed across occurrences) together with frequency into a biased PageRank to score candidate words and phrases.
evidence: Section 3.1: 'we describe PositionRank ... that simultaneously incorporates the position of words and their frequency in a document to compute a biased PageRank score for each candidate word.'
Section 3.1.2: definition and formula for p̃ where each word's weight is the sum of inverse positions of its occurrences and p̃ is normalized and used in PageRank damping term.
Section 3.1.3: phrases formed by concatenating adjacent candidate words and scored as sum of constituent word scores.

Assumes candidate words filtered by POS (nouns, adjectives) are sufficient for capturing keyphrases.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Inverse-of-position (1/position) is an appropriate weighting function to capture the importance of early occurrences; summing these across occurrences adequately balances position and frequency.
supporting_evidence: Section 3.1.2: the authors define word weight as sum of 1/position across occurrences and use that to build p̃.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If 1/position is a poor fit (e.g., too weak/strong decay), PositionRank's preference vector may misrank terms; alternative decay functions might yield different or better results.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: POS filtering to nouns and adjectives (using Stanford NLP) retains the candidate words necessary for gold-standard author keyphrases.
supporting_evidence: Section 3.1.1: 'we select as candidate words only nouns and adjectives, similar to previous works.'
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If many gold keyphrases contain other POS (verbs, proper nouns outside noun/adjective tagging errors), recall will be reduced and reported performance may overstate general effectiveness.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Author-input keyphrases are an adequate gold-standard for evaluation of automatic keyphrase extraction.
supporting_evidence: Section 4.1: 'The author-input keyphrases are used as gold-standard for evaluation.'
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Author keyphrases may be noisy, inconsistent, or incomplete; evaluation against them may bias results (e.g., favoring phrases appearing early) and limit generalizability.

supporting_evidence: Section 4.1 explicitly states only title+abstract used.

identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Stemming may create false matches or miss paraphrases/synonyms; reported precision/recall could be biased by stemming behavior.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The implementation choices and parameter settings for compared baselines (TF-IDF idf estimated from three datasets; ExpandRank neighbors tuned; TPR topic model trained on 45k abstracts) provide a fair and competitive baseline.
supporting_evidence: Section 4.2: descriptions of TF-IDF idf estimation, ExpandRank neighbor selection, and TPR topic model training.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Summing individual word PageRank scores to obtain phrase scores is an effective scoring function for multi-word keyphrases.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes PositionRank, an unsupervised graph-based keyphrase extractor that biases the PageRank teleportation (preference) vector by summing inverse-position weights of all occurrences of each candidate word, combined with standard co-occurrence graph edges and phrase scoring by summing constituent word scores. The empirical claim is that aggregating all positions (PositionRank-full) beats first-position-only, and that PositionRank improves substantially over PageRank baselines (TextRank, SingleRank) and other unsupervised baselines (TF-IDF, ExpandRank, TopicalPageRank) on three scholarly-paper datasets (KDD, WWW, Nguyen) in MRR and P/R/F1, with reported statistical significance. Key supporting experiments include parameter-sensitivity plots (window size w; damping α summary), ablation (full vs first-position), MRR curves vs baselines, and P/R/F1 tables. Core assumptions include the suitability of 1/position weighting, POS filtering to nouns/adjectives, use of title+abstract only, and fairness/implementation parity of baselines. The argument is coherent in that the model design (bias preference toward early+frequent words) directly maps to the hypothesized benefit, and empirical results generally support the main claims; however, several links in the chain lack quantitative detail, reproducibility artifacts, or tests needed to fully validate the claimed causal effects and fairness of comparisons.
logical_argument_graph: Node: Empirical observation — keyphrases tend to appear early and frequently in scholarly documents (Intro, Fig.1) -> Edge -> Motivates position-aware scoring.
Node: Design choice — candidate selection by POS (nouns/adjectives) and graph construction via co-occurrence window w (Sec 3.1.1) -> Edge -> Defines word graph on which ranking operates.
Node: Position weighting — define per-word weight p_i = sum_{occurrences} (1/position) (Sec 3.1.2) -> Edge -> Build biased teleportation vector p̃ by normalizing p_i.
Node: Position-biased PageRank — compute S = α M̃ S + (1-α) p̃ (Sec 3.1.2) -> Edge -> Produces per-word scores incorporating position+frequency and global graph structure.

Node: Phrase formation/scoring — concatenate contiguous candidate words matching (adj)*(noun)+ up to trigram; score phrase = sum word scores (Sec 3.1.3) -> Edge -> Produce ranked keyphrase predictions.
Node: Ablation (full vs first-pos) — compare PositionRank-full to PositionRank-fp (Sec 4.2, Fig 3) -> Edge -> Shows full aggregation yields higher MRR consistently (claim C2).

Node: Baseline comparison — MRR and P/R/F1 vs TextRank, SingleRank, TF-IDF, ExpandRank, TPR (Sec 4.2/4.3, Figs 4,5, Table 2) -> Edge -> PositionRank shows substantial relative improvements and statistical tests claimed (claims C3,C4).

Node: Hyperparameter robustness — vary window w and α (Sec 4.2, Fig 2; α results not shown) -> Edge -> Authors claim low sensitivity (claim C5), but quantitative deltas and statistical measures are limited.

Node: Complexity claim — PositionRank uses only target doc and no external topic models/neighbors, therefore simpler and cheaper than TPR/ExpandRank (Sec 4.3, Conclusion) -> Edge -> Claimed efficiency advantage (claim C6) but lacking measured runtime/memory evidence.

Logical break: Statistical-significance claim -> Missing explicit p-values, per-comparison tests, or multiple-comparison correction; baseline parity details incomplete (window/stoplist/stemming/TPR hyperparams) -> Weakens strength of inference that observed gains stem from algorithmic improvement rather than experimental setup.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes PositionRank: a graph-based unsupervised keyphrase extraction method that biases PageRank's teleport/preference vector using a per-word weight computed by summing inverse document positions (1/position) over all occurrences, combined with standard frequency/co-occurrence edges. Candidate phrases are contiguous noun/adjective sequences up to length three and phrase scores are sums of word PageRank scores. Experiments on three scholarly datasets (title+abstract only) compare PositionRank (full aggregation) against PageRank baselines (TextRank, SingleRank), TF-IDF, ExpandRank, and TopicalPageRank (TPR). Reported outcomes: consistent MRR, P/R/F1 improvements (relative MRR gains up to 29%), ablation showing full aggregation > first-position-only, and claimed robustness to window size and damping factor. Statistical significance (paired t-test, p<0.05) is asserted. Key methodological assumptions include the choice of 1/position weighting and POS filtering (nouns/adjectives), use of author keyphrases as gold standard, and experiments restricted to title+abstract. The main missing reproducibility elements are full numerical results for parameter sweeps, detailed baseline hyperparameters and tuning procedures, per-document outputs for MRR, exact p-values and multiple-comparison handling, and runtime/memory measurements supporting computational-cost claims.
logical_argument_graph: A1: Empirical observation — keyphrases tend to appear early and frequently in scholarly docs -> motivates position weighting.
Design1: Define per-word weight p_i = sum_{occurrences} 1/position -> normalized to form bias vector p̃ for PageRank.
Design2: Build undirected co-occurrence graph with window w and edge weights = co-occurrence counts.
Design3: Compute biased PageRank with damping α and teleport vector p̃ -> word scores S.
Design4: Form candidate phrases via POS-filtered contiguous sequences (adj* noun+) up to length 3; phrase score = sum constituent S.
Experiment1 (Ablation): Compare PositionRank-full vs PositionRank-fp (first-position only) -> full wins in MRR curves.
Experiment2 (Baselines): Compare PositionRank vs TextRank, SingleRank, TF-IDF, ExpandRank, TPR on three datasets -> PositionRank shows higher MRR and P/R/F1.
Claim of robustness: Vary w and α -> performance stable (qualitative claim; some α results not shown).

Claim of simplicity/efficiency: PositionRank uses only target doc vs TPR/ExpandRank needing external corpora/topic training/neighborhood -> claim of lower computational complexity (no empirical costs provided).
Conclusion: Position aggregation into PageRank preference vector provides consistent and significant gains for keyphrase extraction on title+abstract of scholarly documents.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes PositionRank, an unsupervised graph-based keyphrase extraction method that biases PageRank's teleportation (preference) vector using an aggregated inverse-position weight per candidate word (sum over 1/position for each occurrence). Candidate words are nouns/adjectives from title+abstract; phrase scores are sums of constituent word PageRank scores. Empirically, the authors compare PositionRank (full aggregation vs first-position-only) to PageRank variants (TextRank, SingleRank) and other unsupervised baselines (TF-IDF, ExpandRank, TopicalPageRank) on three scholarly-paper datasets (KDD, WWW, Nguyen). They report consistent MRR gains (up to ~29% relative) and statistically significant improvements (paired t-test, p<0.05), claim parameter robustness across window size and damping factor, and argue PositionRank is simpler/cheaper than topic- or neighborhood-based methods. The core incremental idea is to encode position information directly into the PageRank preference vector by summing inverse-position contributions from every occurrence, rather than using only the first occurrence or omitting position entirely. The empirical evidence supports that this specific aggregation improves ranking for title+abstract extraction on the provided datasets, but some methodological and reporting gaps limit how strongly one can attribute gains solely to the proposed design choice.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Keyphrases in scholarly documents tend to appear early and often (observational premise).
P2: Supervised systems use position as a strong feature, but unsupervised PageRank-based models do not typically incorporate full occurrence-position distributions.
A1: A meaningful unsupervised bias can be injected into PageRank by setting the teleportation (preference) vector according to per-word position+frequency weights.
D1: Define weight for word w as sum_{occurrences i} 1/position_i; normalize weights to form preference vector p̃.
D2: Run PageRank with p̃ to obtain word scores; form candidate phrases by concatenating adjacent candidate words and summing constituent scores.
E1: On three datasets, PositionRank-full > PositionRank-fp (ablation), and PositionRank > TextRank/SingleRank/TF-IDF/ExpandRank/TPR in MRR and P/R/F1.
C1: Aggregating all occurrence positions into PageRank's preference vector yields better unsupervised keyphrase ranking on title+abstract extraction for the tested scholarly datasets.
Caveats: Statistical-test reporting, baseline tuning parity, alternative weighting choices, and full-text generalizability are unresolved and could affect the interpretation of E1.

concerns.title: Additive phrase scoring ignores collocation strength

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper argues that position information aggregated across all occurrences of candidate words (via summing inverse-position weights) can be used to bias the PageRank preference vector and thereby improve unsupervised graph-based keyphrase extraction from scholarly documents. Method: build an undirected word co-occurrence graph from title+abstract with window w, compute per-word position-weight p_i = sum_{occurrences} 1/position, normalize p into the PageRank teleport/preference vector p̃, run PageRank with damping α, form candidate phrases by concatenating adjacent nouns/adjectives up to trigrams and score phrases by summing constituent word PageRank scores. Empirical claims: PositionRank-full (all positions) outperforms PositionRank-fp (first position only), TextRank/SingleRank, TF-IDF, ExpandRank and TopicalPageRank on three datasets (KDD, WWW, Nguyen) in MRR and P/R/F1; improvements reported up to ≈29% MRR on Nguyen. Additional claims: parameter robustness to window size and damping factor, and lower complexity/simplicity vs topic/neighborhood methods because PositionRank uses only the target document and no external training. The experimental pipeline uses title+abstract only, POS filtering (nouns/adjectives), Porter stemming, MRR curves, P/R/F1 at top-k, and paired t-tests for significance (p<0.05).
logical_argument_graph: Observation: In scholarly documents, many author keyphrases tend to occur early and often (intro + title/abstract).
Premise: Position and frequency jointly signal importance of candidate terms.
Construction: Build undirected co-occurrence graph from title+abstract; nodes = POS-filtered nouns/adjectives, edges from windowed co-occurrence (w).
Weighting: For each candidate word, compute p_i = sum_{occurrences} 1/position (inverse-position aggregation) to capture early+frequent occurrences.
Integration: Use normalized p vector as the PageRank teleport/preference vector p̃ in a biased PageRank (S = αM̃S + (1−α)p̃).
Phrase formation: assemble adjacent candidate words matching (adjective)*(noun)+ up to trigrams; score phrase by summing constituent word PageRank scores.
Prediction: Rank phrases by score; output top-k as keyphrases.
Ablation: Compare PositionRank-full (sum inverse positions) vs PositionRank-fp (only first occurrence) — full should yield higher MRR.
Evaluation: Test on KDD/WWW/Nguyen datasets versus TextRank, SingleRank, TF-IDF, ExpandRank, TopicalPageRank using MRR and P/R/F1; report statistical significance via paired t-test.

Conclusion: Position-aggregation biasing of PageRank yields substantial, statistically significant gains while remaining simple and (claimed) computationally cheaper than topic/neighborhood approaches.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes PositionRank, an unsupervised graph-based keyphrase extraction method that biases the PageRank teleportation (preference) vector using per-word weights equal to the sum over occurrences of 1/position (inverse-position aggregation), combined with standard co-occurrence edges and phrase scoring by summing constituent word PageRank scores. The central empirical argument is that aggregating position information from all occurrences (PositionRank-full) yields consistent improvements over: (a) PageRank variants that ignore position (TextRank, SingleRank), (b) a first-position-only variant (PositionRank-fp), and (c) other unsupervised baselines (TF-IDF, ExpandRank, TopicalPageRank) on three scholarly-paper datasets (KDD, WWW, Nguyen), measured by MRR and P/R/F1. The paper supplies MRR curves, parameter sensitivity plots for window size (w), an ablation for full vs first-position aggregation, and a P/R/F1 table; it asserts paired t-test significance (p < 0.05) and claims PositionRank is simpler/cheaper than topic/neighborhood-based methods. The manuscript's reasoning chain is: (1) author keyphrases tend to appear early and repeat; (2) encode early occurrence and frequency as summed inverse-position weights to form a biased teleport vector p̃; (3) run PageRank with p̃ to elevate early+frequent terms; (4) aggregate word scores into phrases and rank. Empirical results presented generally support improved ranking and extraction effectiveness. However, several evidentiary and methodological gaps limit how decisively the claims can be attributed solely to the proposed design: missing exact p-values and effect sizes for key comparisons, incomplete reporting of baseline hyperparameters and tuning, lack of runtime/memory measurements to substantiate efficiency claims, and no exploration of alternative position-weighting functions or evaluations beyond title+abstract and noun/adjective candidate filtering. I mark supported, partially supported, and overstated parts in the detailed claims below and provide specific, evidence-based suggestions and uncertainty notes.
logical_argument_graph: Observation: Keyphrases in scholarly documents tend to occur early and recur across the document (Section 1, Figure 1).
Design decision: Represent candidate words as nodes in a co-occurrence graph (w-window) and build undirected weighted edges (Section 3.1.1).
Position encoding: For each word, compute p_i = sum_{occurrences} 1/position and normalize to form teleport vector p̃ (Section 3.1.2).
Ranking mechanism: Run biased PageRank S = α M̃ S + (1−α) p̃ to obtain word importance (Section 3.1.2).
Phrase formation: Concatenate contiguous noun/adjective candidates (adj* noun+) up to trigrams and score phrases by summing constituent word PageRank scores (Section 3.1.3).
Ablation: Compare PositionRank-full vs PositionRank-fp to isolate contribution of aggregating all positions (Section 4.2, Figure 3).
Baselines comparison: Compare to TextRank, SingleRank, TF-IDF, ExpandRank, TopicalPageRank using MRR and P/R/F1 (Section 4.2–4.3, Figures 4–5, Table 2).
Claim: PositionRank improves MRR and P/R/F1 across datasets (Section 4.2–4.3; relative improvements reported and paired t-test p<0.05).
Robustness: Vary window size w and damping α; report minimal sensitivity for w (Figure 2) and state α variations not significant (results not shown).
Efficiency claim: PositionRank simpler/cheaper because it uses only target document vs TPR/ExpandRank that require external data (Section 4.3, Conclusion).

identified_claims.claim_label: Design: PositionRank sums inverse positions into PageRank preference
identified_claims.claim_text: PositionRank is an unsupervised graph-based model that incorporates information from all positions of a word's occurrences (via inverse-position weights summed across occurrences) together with frequency into a biased PageRank to score candidate words and phrases.
evidence: Section 3.1: explicit description of PositionRank incorporating position and frequency.
Section 3.1.2: formal definition of p_i = sum_{occurrences} 1/position and p̃ normalization; Equation 2 uses p̃ in PageRank.
uncertainty_flags: Choice of 1/position as weighting function presented without empirical justification or comparison to alternatives.
Normalization of p̃ described but sensitivity to normalization scheme not analyzed.

identified_claims.claim_text: Aggregating position information from all occurrences of a word (PositionRank-full) outperforms using only the first occurrence position (PositionRank-fp).
identified_claims.section_anchor: 4.2 'What is the impact...' and Figure 3
evidence: Figure 3 reported: PositionRank-full consistently outperforms PositionRank-fp across KDD, WWW, Nguyen MRR curves.
Section 4.2: textual claim that full model 'consistently outperforms' first-position-only counterpart.
uncertainty_flags: No numeric effect sizes or statistical tests reported specifically for this ablation; only visual MRR curves.
Alternative aggregation functions (e.g., exponential decay, 1/position^beta) not explored; result may be specific to 1/position summation.

identified_claims.claim_text: PositionRank substantially outperforms PageRank-based baselines that ignore position (TextRank, SingleRank) on KDD, WWW, and Nguyen datasets in MRR (and P/R/F1), with reported relative improvements (e.g., MRR@avg_k improvements of 17–20% over SingleRank).
identified_claims.section_anchor: 4.2 'How well does position information aid...' Figure 4; Table 2
evidence: Figure 4: MRR curves show PositionRank above TextRank/SingleRank.
Section 4.2: quoted relative improvement percentages over SingleRank for each dataset.
Table 2: P/R/F1 rows show PositionRank rows marked best.
uncertainty_flags: Paired t-test significance is asserted but exact p-values for these specific comparisons and which metrics/k values tested are not provided.

Baseline implementations and hyperparameters (window sizes, preprocessing parity) are described briefly but not exhaustively, leaving small risk of implementation/configuration differences contributing to gains.

identified_claims.claim_text: PositionRank outperforms several strong unsupervised baselines (TF-IDF, ExpandRank, TopicalPageRank) on the three scholarly datasets, with relative improvements in MRR up to ~29% (Nguyen).
identified_claims.section_anchor: 4.2 'How does PositionRank compare...' Figure 5; 4.3 Table 2; Conclusion
evidence: Figure 5: MRR curves comparing PositionRank and baselines show PositionRank leading across datasets.
Section 4.2: statement of highest relative improvement 29.09% on Nguyen.
Table 2: PositionRank achieves highest P/R/F1 for top-k columns shown.
uncertainty_flags: TPR required external topic model trained on 45k abstracts; details of topic count and tuning are not fully enumerated, which could affect TPR performance.
ExpandRank neighborhood size was tuned but only best results shown; absence of full tuning curves reduces transparency.
No runtime/memory benchmarks provided to validate computational-cost claims comparing PositionRank to these methods.

identified_claims.claim_text: PositionRank is robust to hyperparameter choices: window size w (tested 2..10) and damping factor α (0.75..0.9) do not significantly change performance.

evidence: Figure 2: MRR curves for different values of w showing overlapping performance.
Section 4.2: statement that α variations were tested and 'did not find significant differences' (results not shown).
uncertainty_flags: No numerical deltas, confidence intervals, or formal statistical tests shown for w sensitivity; α results not shown at all.
Robustness claim uses qualitative language; reproducibility requires presenting the withheld α curves and numeric summaries.

identified_claims.claim_text: PositionRank is simpler and computationally cheaper than topic-based (TopicalPageRank) or neighborhood-expanded approaches (ExpandRank) because it uses only the target document and no external training, while achieving better or comparable performance.

evidence: Discussion in Section 4.3 contrasts PositionRank (single-document) with TPR (requires topic model training) and ExpandRank (uses textual neighborhood).
Abstract and Conclusion explicitly assert simplicity and computational advantage.
uncertainty_flags: No empirical runtime/memory/complexity measurements were provided to quantify 'computationally cheaper'; claim is plausible but unmeasured.
ExpandRank/TPR implementations and their computational footprints are not specified; 'cheaper' is qualitative and depends on parameters and dataset sizes.

strengths.title: Clear, focused algorithmic idea linking observation to mechanism
strengths.description: The paper presents a simple, well-specified mechanism (sum of inverse positions into PageRank preference) that directly operationalizes the observation that scholarly keyphrases tend to appear early and repeat.
evidence: Section 1 motivating example and Figure 1.
Section 3.1.2 formal definition of p_i = sum 1/position and Equation 2 integrating p̃ into PageRank.

strengths.title: Targeted ablation isolating the main design choice
strengths.description: The comparison between PositionRank-full and PositionRank-fp isolates the contribution of aggregating all occurrence positions versus only first occurrence, providing focused evidence for the central hypothesis.
evidence: Section 4.2 and Figure 3 showing full consistently above fp.
Textual discussion drawing the conclusion to use full model for further experiments.

strengths.title: Broad baseline set and multi-dataset evaluation
strengths.description: Experiments compare PositionRank to multiple competitive unsupervised baselines (TextRank, SingleRank, TF-IDF, ExpandRank, TopicalPageRank) across three datasets, supporting generality within the scholarly paper setting.
evidence: Figures 4 and 5; Table 2 include multiple baselines and datasets (KDD, WWW, Nguyen).
Section 4.1 description of datasets and metrics (MRR, P/R/F1).

strengths.title: Practical, easily implementable method
strengths.description: PositionRank requires only standard preprocessing (POS filtering, co-occurrence graph) and a PageRank run; the algorithm is reproducible from the paper and likely fast in single-document settings.
evidence: Section 3 describes graph construction, PageRank equation, and phrase formation in implementable detail.
Use of standard components (Stanford POS tagger, Porter stemmer, PageRank) reduces barrier to reproduction.

concerns.title: Incomplete statistical reporting and significance scope
concerns.description: The paper asserts paired t-test significance (p < 0.05) for improvements but does not report exact p-values, which specific comparisons were tested (which datasets, metrics, and k-values), effect sizes, or checks of test assumptions (normality) and multiple-comparisons correction.
evidence: Section 4.3: 'With a paired t-test on our results, we found that the improvements ... are statistically significant (p-values < 0.05).' No per-comparison p-values or test details shown.
Ablation and sensitivity claims lack per-experiment statistical reporting.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide per-comparison statistics: exact p-values, test statistics, effect sizes (e.g., Cohen's d), confidence intervals; report which measures and k-values were tested; if assumptions of t-test are questionable, report non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank) and apply corrections for multiple comparisons (e.g., Holm-Bonferroni).

concerns.title: Baseline configuration and reproducibility transparency
concerns.description: Implementations and hyperparameters for baselines (TopicalPageRank: number of topics, Mallet settings; ExpandRank: neighborhood size and similarity measure; TF-IDF: idf corpus details) are not exhaustively listed, hindering reproducibility and raising fairness concerns.
evidence: Section 4.2 mentions training TPR topic model on ~45k abstracts using Mallet but omits number of topics and other Mallet parameters.
ExpandRank: 'various numbers of textually-similar neighbors' tested but only best results shown; no per-parameter results or chosen neighbor counts listed.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include full hyperparameter tables for all baselines (topic counts, alpha priors, neighbor counts, similarity thresholds), supply code/config files or link to released implementations, and report tuning procedure (grid ranges and validation method).

concerns.title: Unjustified position-weighting functional choice
concerns.description: The model uses 1/position summed across occurrences as the sole position-weighting function; no experiments explore alternative formulations (e.g., exponential decay, 1/position^beta, log-based weighting) or verify that the chosen form is optimal or robust.
evidence: Section 3.1.2 defines 1/position and presents an illustrative example but offers no empirical comparison to other decay functions.
Shared analysis and prior-stage digests note absence of alternative position-weight experiments.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run and report ablations testing at least 2–3 alternative position-weighting schemes (e.g., exp(−β·position), 1/position^β with β tuned, or normalized decay) and present comparative MRR/P/R/F1 results to justify 1/position or report sensitivity.

concerns.title: Missing runtime and complexity measurements
concerns.description: The claim that PositionRank is computationally cheaper than topic-based (TPR) or neighborhood-expanded (ExpandRank) approaches is left qualitative with no runtime, memory, or complexity analyses presented.
evidence: Section 4.3 and Conclusion assert PositionRank is 'much less complex' and 'does not require an additional dataset' but provide no timing or memory metrics.
ExpandRank and TPR descriptions suggest higher cost but without quantified comparisons.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Measure and report wall-clock runtime and peak memory for PositionRank, TPR, and ExpandRank on the same hardware and dataset sizes; include complexity discussion (per-document cost vs corpus-level preprocessing) and, if possible, scale experiments on increasing document sizes or neighborhood sizes.

concerns.title: Evaluation limited to title+abstract and POS filter may bias results
concerns.description: Experiments are restricted to title and abstract text and candidate selection filters to nouns/adjectives, which may bias results toward early-occurring keyphrases and limit generalizability to full-text or other genres; no analysis shows how many gold keyphrases are excluded by the POS filter or by using only title+abstract.
evidence: Section 4.1: experiments use only title+abstract and author-input keyphrases as gold standard.
Shared analysis points out potential bias: author keyphrases and title+abstract emphasize early occurrences.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report coverage statistics: proportion of gold author keyphrases that appear in title+abstract and proportion passing the POS filter (noun/adjective). If possible, evaluate on full text for a subset to quantify degradation or generalization; at minimum, discuss limitations and expected effects of the constrained input.

concerns.title: Incomplete parameter sensitivity reporting (α results withheld)
concerns.description: Window-size sensitivity (w) is presented but without numerical deltas or confidence; damping factor α experiments are claimed but results not shown ('results not shown'), reducing verifiability.
evidence: Section 4.2: Figure 2 shows w sensitivity qualitatively; Section states α values tested but 'results not shown due to highly overlapping curves.'
No numeric summary (mean/std) across parameter settings is included.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide numeric tables or error bars for MRR across w values and include the α sensitivity curves or a small table summarizing mean and variance so readers can verify 'not significant' claim.

comparable_works.relevance: Primary PageRank-based unsupervised baseline used for comparison.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: TextRank uses uniform teleport vector and adjacency from adjacency co-occurrence (w=2). PositionRank differs by biasing teleport vector using position aggregation.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 2 Related Work; comparison in Section 4.2 and Figure 4.

comparable_works.relevance: PageRank extension adding weighted co-occurrence window (SingleRank) and neighborhood expansion (ExpandRank); used as strong baselines.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: SingleRank shares co-occurrence window idea; ExpandRank adds textual neighbors. PositionRank instead biases teleport vector using position information and is single-document only.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 2 and Section 4.2 discussion; Table 2 results where ExpandRank is competitive.

comparable_works.relevance: Represents topic-biased PageRank approaches using topic models; strongest extrinsic-data baseline.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: TPR uses topic decomposition and topic-biased teleport vectors; PositionRank uses position-biased teleport vector without topic models. TPR requires external topic model training (45k abstracts in experiments).
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 2 Related Work; Section 4.2 methodological description (Mallet; 45k abstracts).

comparable_works.relevance: Simple lexical baseline widely used in prior work and included in comparisons.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: TF-IDF ranks words by statistical weighting over corpus (idf estimated from datasets); PositionRank uses structural graph + position bias to capture centrality and early occurrence.

uncertainty_flags: Statistical testing: exact p-values, which comparisons tested, effect sizes, and multiple-comparison corrections are not reported.
Baseline parity: full hyperparameters for TopicalPageRank, ExpandRank, and TF-IDF idf corpus specification are incompletely documented.
Position-weighting: 1/position chosen without comparison to alternative decay functions; results may be sensitive to this choice.
α sensitivity: experiments were run but results withheld; numerical summaries are missing.
Evaluation scope: title+abstract-only and POS filtering may bias results toward early-occurring phrases and reduce generality to full-text extraction.
alternative_interpretations: Improvements attributed to position aggregation may partly stem from the constrained evaluation (title+abstract and author keyphrases) where early occurrences are over-represented; in full-text conditions the advantage might shrink.

Performance gains over complex baselines (TPR, ExpandRank) could be influenced by suboptimal baseline hyperparameter choices or resource constraints (e.g., number of topics, neighbor sizes); with different tuning, gaps might narrow.

Summing 1/position may have the side-effect of implicitly favoring high-frequency tokens that occur early; some improvements could reflect frequency effects already captured by other baselines and the specific normalization choices used.
The reported robustness to parameters may hold only within the narrow experimental setting (title+abstract and three datasets) and may not generalize to other corpora or full texts.
transparency_notes: Authors provide clear algorithmic equations and dataset descriptions, enabling re-implementation of PositionRank, but omit many baseline hyperparameters and exact statistical outputs.

Key experimental artifacts to request: code for PositionRank, scripts for preprocessing (POS tagging, stemming), configuration files for TPR/ExpandRank runs, per-document ranked outputs used to compute MRR so replication of paired tests is possible.
Alpha sensitivity results are stated but not presented; providing these plots or numeric tables would increase reproducibility and trust in robustness claims.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: Although encoding position into PageRank preference is an incremental modification of prior PageRank-based keyphrase extractors, aggregating inverse positions across all occurrences (rather than first occurrence or none) appears novel in the unsupervised literature recorded in the manuscript. Novelty here does not automatically validate effectiveness — empirical and statistical rigor are required to separate genuine algorithmic advantage from evaluation artifacts.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If author keyphrases frequently appear early in title+abstract (high coverage), the position-biased teleport vector will likely help the ranking and MRR metrics.
If baseline implementations are properly tuned and PositionRank still holds advantages across full text and other document genres, the method would be robust and broadly useful.
If alternative position-weight functions (e.g., exponential decay) produce similar or superior gains, the core idea (position bias) remains valuable even if 1/position is not uniquely optimal.

novelty_lenses.rationale: PositionRank modifies the teleport vector of PageRank to incorporate a summed inverse-position weight; this is an intuitive but previously untested way to encode position information in unsupervised PageRank-based extractors, representing a focused incremental contribution rather than a paradigm shift.
evidence: Section 3.1.2 describes the exact modification (p_i = sum 1/position).
Related work notes that supervised models use first-position but prior unsupervised work did not incorporate full position aggregation.
uncertainty_flags: Novelty depends on completeness of literature; manuscript claims 'to our knowledge' novelty, but absent exhaustive retrieval this remains a best-effort claim.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Empirical results across three datasets show consistent improvements in MRR and P/R/F1, but incomplete statistical reporting and baseline tuning transparency limit the strength of causal attribution solely to the proposed method.
evidence: Figures 3–5 and Table 2 show consistent visual and tabulated performance advantages.
Section 4.3 asserts paired t-test significance (p<0.05) though without per-comparison details.
uncertainty_flags: Exact p-values, effect sizes, and baseline hyperparameter parity not provided.

confidence_interval.rationale: This 'confidence interval' field is used to indicate the reviewer's overall calibration of certainty about the paper's claims given the available evidence and the noted gaps. The evidence supports that PositionRank yields improvements in the experimental setting presented, but methodological gaps (statistical reporting, baseline parity, alternative weighting functions, runtime measures, limited evaluation scope) leave substantial uncertainty about the generality and sole cause of the observed gains. Therefore, a bounded numeric confidence is not appropriate; I provide qualitative judgments and high/medium/low confidences in specific findings above.

consensus_findings: PositionRank is a clearly specified modification of PageRank: the teleportation (preference) vector is built from per-word weights equal to the sum of inverse occurrence positions (1/position) and normalized, and phrases are scored by summing constituent word PageRank scores.

The authors present an ablation showing that aggregating position information from all occurrences (PositionRank-full) yields better MRR than using only the first occurrence (PositionRank-fp) on the three reported scholarly datasets (KDD, WWW, Nguyen).

PositionRank shows consistent empirical improvements over several unsupervised baselines (TextRank, SingleRank, TF-IDF, ExpandRank, TopicalPageRank) on the reported title+abstract scholarly datasets in MRR and in P/R/F1 tables/curves as presented in the paper.

The paper's experimental pipeline is reproducible in principle: datasets, high-level preprocessing (title+abstract only, POS filtering to nouns/adjectives, Porter stemming), PageRank formula and parameters (default damping 0.85) are described sufficiently to implement the core method.

There are important reporting and methodological gaps common to all reviewers that limit the strength of empirical claims: incomplete statistical reporting (no per-comparison p-values/effect sizes or multiple-comparison handling), limited baseline hyperparameter transparency, absent runtime/memory measurements, and lack of experiments exploring alternative position-weighting functions or broader evaluation beyond title+abstract.
disagreements: Magnitude and generality of the empirical improvement: reviewers differ in confidence about how broadly the reported gains will generalize beyond the specific experimental setup. Some find the gains plausibly robust within the title+abstract scholarly setting, while others caution that the effect size and generality are uncertain without additional analyses (alternative weighting functions, full-text evaluation, stricter baseline parity).

Novelty framing: some reviewers emphasize that the contribution is a meaningful, implementable incremental innovation within PageRank-based extractors (novelty signal), while another reviewer flags that the idea is disruptive only if prior unsupervised uses of full-position aggregation are indeed absent; they differ on how strongly to emphasize novelty vs incremental improvement.

Severity assigned to missing computational-cost measurements: some reviewers treat the absence of runtime/memory profiling as a moderate methodological flaw that weakens the efficiency claim; others treat it as a lower-severity omission that can be remedied in revision.
uncertainty_hotspots: Statistical testing and reported significance: exact p-values, test statistics, which metric-dataset-k comparisons were tested, normality checks, and multiple-comparison corrections are not provided. This prevents confident interpretation of 'statistically significant' statements.

Baseline parity and tuning transparency: key baseline hyperparameters (TopicalPageRank topic counts and Mallet settings, ExpandRank neighbor counts and similarity thresholds, TF-IDF idf corpus composition) and implementation details are insufficiently documented, making it unclear whether observed advantages stem from method or from tuning/implementation differences.

Position-weight functional form: the chosen weight (sum of 1/position) is not compared to alternative decays (e.g., 1/position^beta, exponential) or normalization strategies; sensitivity of results to this design choice is unknown.

Evaluation scope and potential gold-standard bias: experiments use only title+abstract and author-supplied keyphrases; since author keyphrases often overlap early-occurring title/abstract terms, this evaluation regime may elevate apparent gains from position bias compared to full-text or other gold-standards.
Computational-cost claims: 'simpler and computationally cheaper' is asserted without measured wall-clock or memory metrics or amortization accounting for TPR/ExpandRank training/preprocessing.
Parameter-robustness evidence incomplete: window-size plots lack variance/error measures and damping-factor (α) results are asserted but not shown, reducing confidence in robustness claims.
model_diversity_effects: Structure_Analyst role effect: emphasizes logical coherence and internal causal chain (position -> preference vector -> PageRank effect) and highlights reproducibility gaps that weaken causal attribution; flags missing statistical detail as a major methodological flaw.

Methodology_Auditor role effect: focuses on reproducibility and validity, pushing for release of code, per-document outputs, and precisely reported hyperparameters; elevates concerns about baseline parity and test assumptions.
Novelty_Assessor (incremental) effect: frames the work as a targeted incremental change with clear implementation utility; stresses experimental gains but asks for broader robustness checks.
Novelty_Assessor (disruptive) effect: treats the idea as potentially conceptually novel for unsupervised PageRank-based extractors, urging careful literature framing and caveated novelty claims.

Net effect: role diversity results in complementary criticisms—logical coherence and empirical signals are accepted, while reproducibility, statistical rigor, and generality are repeatedly flagged—producing a multi-faceted but non-uniform view that maintains controlled disagreement rather than collapsing into a single verdict.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Maintain editorial centrality: request a revision that addresses the core transparency and robustness gaps before relying on the reported empirical magnitudes. Specifically, ask the authors to (1) provide exact statistical test results (per-comparison p-values, test statistics, sample sizes, effect sizes, confidence intervals), include checks for test assumptions (normality) or non-parametric alternatives, and report or correct for multiple comparisons; (2) publish code and preprocessing scripts, baseline implementations with explicit hyperparameter tables (TPR topic counts and Mallet settings, ExpandRank neighbor counts and similarity measure, TF-IDF idf corpus composition), and the per-document ranked outputs used to compute MRR and P/R/F1 so reviewers can reproduce results and re-run statistical tests; (3) include empirical runtime and memory measurements (per-document or amortized costs) for PositionRank and the major baselines, with hardware details; (4) run additional ablations: alternative position-weighting functions (e.g., 1/position^beta with grid over beta, exponential decay), and report numeric sensitivity for window size w and damping factor α (means ± std or confidence intervals over documents); (5) report coverage diagnostics: what fraction of gold keyphrases are present in title+abstract and survive the POS candidate-filtering (nouns/adjectives), and, if feasible, run a small full-text or different-gold-standard experiment to test generality. Use these additions to re-evaluate claims about significance, robustness, generality and computational cost. Preserve authors' core contribution in revision if the additional evidence supports it; otherwise, request clearer qualification in claims. The editor should treat the current empirical claims as promising but not yet fully substantiated for broad generalization.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript and address reviewers' concerns, provide the following in the revision and supplementary materials: (1) Exact statistical reporting: per-comparison test statistics and p-values, effect sizes (e.g., mean differences, Cohen's d), confidence intervals, sample sizes, and whether tests' assumptions hold; if many tests were run, apply and report multiple-comparison corrections or present non-parametric alternatives (Wilcoxon signed-rank) alongside t-tests. (2) Reproducibility package: release code, preprocessing scripts (tokenizer, POS-tagging version/options, stemming), configuration files for all baselines (TPR topic counts and Mallet parameters, ExpandRank neighbor counts and similarity threshold, TF-IDF idf source), random seeds, and the per-document ranked outputs used to compute MRR/P/R/F1. (3) Position-weight sensitivity: run ablations comparing alternative decay functions (1/position^beta with several β, exponential decay with tunable λ, simple binary early-window indicator), and report results in main text or supplement to justify the chosen 1/position formulation. (4) Robustness numerics: provide numeric tables or plots with means ± standard deviations (or confidence bands) for window-size sweeps and for damping factor α (include the previously 'not shown' α results). (5) Coverage and generality diagnostics: report what fraction of gold keyphrases appear in title+abstract and pass candidate filtering; if possible, add at least one experiment on a subset of full-texts or on a dataset with different annotation style to test generality. (6) Computational profiling: measure and report wall-clock runtime and peak memory for PositionRank and for TPR/ExpandRank (include the training cost of TPR amortized per-document), on comparable hardware. (7) Clarify novelty claims and related work: state explicitly that full-occurrence position aggregation into PageRank's preference vector is (to your knowledge) novel in the unsupervised PageRank family, but couch claims cautiously and cite any close analogs. These actions will allow reviewers and readers to verify significance, fairness, and generality of claims and will materially strengthen the manuscript's evidentiary basis.
transparency_report: Statistical reporting: paired t-test significance is asserted (p < 0.05) but exact p-values, per-comparison scope, effect sizes, confidence intervals, and multiple-comparison handling are not provided.

Baseline configuration: high-level descriptions of baseline setups are included (e.g., TPR trained on ~45k abstracts, ExpandRank neighbors 'tuned for best results') but precise hyperparameters (number of topics, neighbor counts, Mallet options, idf corpus composition) are not tabulated or released.

Preprocessing details: tokenizer, POS tagger (Stanford NLP) and POS tags filtered (nouns/adjectives), and Porter stemming are reported; versions, options, and stopword lists are not fully enumerated in the manuscript.
Per-document outputs: raw per-document ranked lists used to compute MRR and P/R/F1 are not provided, preventing independent recomputation of metric distributions and paired tests.
Parameter sweeps: window-size w sensitivity is plotted qualitatively (Figure 2) but lacks numeric variance/error bars; damping factor (α) experiments are referenced but results are not shown.
Position-weighting alternatives: only the 1/position summed scheme is presented; no experiments test alternate decay or normalization schemes.
Runtime/memory reporting: no empirical measurements or amortized comparisons are provided to substantiate 'computationally cheaper' claims.
epistemic_limits: The synthesis and reviewers' assessments are bounded by the information present in the manuscript and the shared analyses. We cannot observe the authors' code, raw outputs, or withheld numerical results; therefore attributions about causal sources of empirical gains (algorithmic innovation vs experimental setup/baseline tuning vs evaluation bias) remain tentative. Statistical-significance claims cannot be independently validated without per-document metric vectors and exact test parameters. Generalization beyond the tested title+abstract scholarly datasets (to full text or other genres) is unknown because experiments are limited to a narrow input scope and gold-standard style (author keyphrases). Claims about computational cost are qualitative in absence of runtime/memory measurements and amortized analyses. Finally, absence of experiments exploring alternative position-weight functions prevents concluding that the chosen 1/position formulation is optimal; it should be treated as a plausible design choice pending sensitivity analyses.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript introduces PositionRank, an unsupervised graph-based keyphrase extraction method that biases PageRank's teleportation (preference) vector using per-word weights equal to the sum of inverse occurrence positions (1/position) across a document. Candidate words are POS-filtered (nouns/adjectives) from title+abstract, a co-occurrence graph is built with window w, PageRank is run with the position-derived preference vector, and multiword phrases are scored by summing constituent word scores. Empirical results on three scholarly-paper collections (KDD, WWW, Nguyen) show that (a) aggregating all occurrence positions (PositionRank-full) yields higher MRR than using only the first position (PositionRank-fp); and (b) PositionRank outperforms several unsupervised baselines (TextRank, SingleRank, TF-IDF, ExpandRank, TopicalPageRank) in reported MRR and P/R/F1, with asserted paired t-test significance (p < 0.05). Reviewers agree the algorithmic idea is clear and implementable and that the ablation and multi-baseline evaluation are appropriate, but they also identify important reporting, reproducibility, and generality gaps that limit interpretability and broader generalization.
strengths: Clear, focused algorithmic contribution: the paper precisely defines per-word position-weighting (sum of 1/position), its normalization into a PageRank preference vector, and the pipeline (graph construction, PageRank, phrase scoring), enabling reimplementation from the text (Sections 3.1, 3.1.2, 3.1.3).

Ablation isolates the core idea: PositionRank-full vs PositionRank-fp is evaluated and PositionRank-full consistently shows improved MRR across the three datasets (Fig. 3), strengthening the causal link between aggregating occurrences and performance.

Empirical comparisons span multiple, relevant unsupervised baselines (TextRank, SingleRank, TF-IDF, ExpandRank, TopicalPageRank) and multiple datasets, showing consistent gains in MRR and P/R/F1 as presented (Figs. 4–5, Table 2).
limitations: Incomplete statistical reporting: the manuscript asserts significance via paired t-tests (p < 0.05) but does not report exact p-values, per-comparison test scopes (which dataset/metric/k were tested), effect sizes, confidence intervals, or checks for test assumptions and multiple-comparison corrections (Section 4.3).

Baseline parity and reproducibility gaps: key baseline hyperparameters and implementation details are under-specified (TopicalPageRank topic counts and Mallet settings; ExpandRank neighbor counts and similarity measures; TF-IDF idf corpus composition), and code/ per-document outputs for MRR/P/R/F1 are not provided, making it hard to rule out tuning/implementation differences as contributors to the reported gains (Section 4.2).

Position-weighting choice underexplored: the specific functional form (sum of 1/position) is presented without comparison to alternative decay families (e.g., 1/position^β, exponential) or normalization variants; sensitivity to this design choice is unreported, so optimality or robustness of 1/position is unknown (Section 3.1.2).

Narrow evaluation scope and possible gold-standard bias: experiments use title+abstract only and author-provided keyphrases as gold; because author keyphrases often reflect early occurrences, the evaluation regime may amplify benefits of a position-biased model and may not reflect performance on full-text or other genres (Section 4.1).
open_questions: Please provide exact statistical test outputs: for each reported claim (MRR, P/R/F1 at each k, dataset), supply test statistic, exact p-value, sample size, effect size (e.g., mean difference and Cohen's d), and state any multiple-comparison correction used—or justify its omission.

Please release code and experimental artifacts: preprocessing scripts (tokenizer, POS tagger version/options, stopword lists), PositionRank implementation, baseline implementations or config files (TPR topic count, Mallet options, ExpandRank neighbor sizes and similarity metric, TF-IDF idf corpus), random seeds, and per-document predicted ranked lists used to compute MRR/P/R/F1.

How sensitive are results to the position-weight functional form? Provide experiments comparing at least a small set of alternatives (1/position^β with β grid, exponential decay exp(-λ·position), and a frequency-only baseline) and report numeric deltas and significance.

human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
PositionRank defines a position-informed PageRank preference vector by summing inverse occurrence positions for each candidate word, normalizing that vector, running PageRank on a standard co-occurrence graph, and scoring phrases by summing constituent word scores. On three scholarly title+abstract datasets, PositionRank-full (all-occurrence aggregation) outperforms a first-position-only variant and several unsupervised baselines in MRR and P/R/F1 as presented.

Strengths:
- The idea is concise, well-specified, and easy to implement (Sections 3.1, 3.1.2, 3.1.3). Equations and examples clarify the algorithm.
- The ablation (full vs first-position) directly tests the core contribution and shows consistent empirical gains (Fig. 3).
- Empirical evaluation includes multiple competitive unsupervised baselines and three datasets, providing a robust-in-appearance testing ground (Figs. 4–5, Table 2).

Limitations:
- Missing statistical detail: exact p-values, per-comparison scopes, effect sizes, confidence intervals, and multiple-comparison handling are not reported (Section 4.3). This prevents independent verification of 'statistical significance'.
- Baseline and reproducibility gaps: key hyperparameters (TPR topic counts, Mallet settings, ExpandRank neighbor counts, TF-IDF idf corpus) and code/ per-document outputs are not provided, making fairness and reproducibility uncertain (Section 4.2).
- Unexplored position-weight alternatives: only sum of 1/position is tested; no results for other decays (1/position^β, exponential) or normalization schemes are reported, leaving the chosen function unjustified (Section 3.1.2).
- Evaluation scope limited to title+abstract and noun/adjective filtering, which can bias results toward early-occurring terms and may not generalize to full-text extraction or other gold standards (Section 4.1).

Open Questions:
- Provide per-comparison statistical outputs (exact p-values, test statistics, sample sizes, effect sizes, CIs) and specify which metrics/datasets/k were tested; if many tests were run, report multiple-comparison corrections or justify omission.
- Release code, preprocessing scripts, baseline configs, random seeds, and the per-document ranked outputs used to compute MRR/P/R/F1 to enable reproduction and independent reanalysis.
- How do alternative position-weighting functions (1/position^β, exponential decay, simple frequency-only) perform relative to sum(1/position)? Please supply numeric comparisons and sensitivity analyses.
- What fraction of gold keyphrases are covered by title+abstract and by the POS candidate filter? If possible, include at least one experiment on full text or another gold standard to assess generality.

Transparency:
The algorithm and high-level experimental design are transparent and reproducible in principle, but essential replication artifacts are missing: exact statistical outputs, complete baseline hyperparameter tables, per-document outputs, withheld α sensitivity data, and runtime/memory measurements. Providing these will materially improve verifiability.

confidence_interval.rationale: Given the presented ablation and multi-baseline experiments, there is moderate-to-high confidence that aggregating occurrence positions into a PageRank preference vector can improve keyphrase ranking in the reported title+abstract scholarly setting. Confidence is limited by incomplete statistical reporting, baseline parity transparency, absent alternative weighting experiments, and narrow evaluation scope. If authors supply the recommended analyses and artifacts, confidence in generality and effect-size claims should increase toward the upper bound.
